front.title: Decision Provenance for SCITT: binding software releases and agent actions to the decisions behind them

abstract.t: A software supply chain records what was built, from what, and by whom: build attestations, bills of materials, signed statements registered in a Transparency Service. It does not record the decision to ship: who approved the release, on what authority, what they were shown, which options were weighed and why. The statement profiles that record AI agent actions have the same gap, and say so: their human-approval fields are the producer's claim. This document describes how a decision record and its action-binding attachment, as the extension proposals of the Decision Provenance Standard define them, sit under both kinds of record by typed digest references; how a verifier checks offline the approval stage, the approver's signature where one is carried, and the chain of digests from what the attachment says was shown to what was executed; and how the witness checkpoints of the anchoring extension are registered in a SCITT Transparency Service. A software release decision is the first worked example and an agent action capsule the second; the model has no feature specific to either. This document is independent of the Decision Provenance Standard, is not part of it, does not change it, and is not endorsed by its Steward.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The SCITT use cases and the formats a software supply chain already carries, build provenance , attestations and bills of materials , answer the question "what is this artifact, and how was it built". Registered as Signed Statements in a Transparency Service , with Receipts , they become evidence anyone can check later. None of them answers "who decided to ship it, on what, and under which authority": the release decision is a ticket, a chat message or a button, and the record of it, where one exists, is neither signed by the decider nor bound to the artifact that shipped.

The statement profiles written for AI agent actions have the same gap, and are careful to say so. A capsule records an action's disposition ; an AgentInteractionRecord its inputs and outcomes ; a receipt its risk class and verdict . Each says that its human-approval field is the producer's claim: an enumeration value or an opaque label, not an authenticated act, and that the reasoning behind the action stays private or reduced to a hash.

The Decision Provenance Standard records the decision: what was decided, under which charter, which options were considered and with what rationale, and the affirmative human act that closed the record. Its action binding extension , a proposal in the Standard's repository, records the stages from a proposed action specification to its execution: what the attachment states the reviewer was shown, what was approved, signed where a signature is carried, what was requested, re-checked and executed, bound to one another by equal digests. Its anchoring extension , also a proposal, gives those records evidence that their bytes existed by a given point, and witness checkpoints, including, since its SCITT source, a witness-signed checkpoint registered in a Transparency Service with its Receipt. A deploy pipeline and an AI agent are two executors of decisions; the Standard does not distinguish them.

This document does three things. It declares two artifact types so that a build attestation, a release statement or an agent action record may cite, by typed digest reference , the decision record and the action-binding attachment it executes. It describes how a verifier holding both checks the approval and the binding offline. And it describes the registration of the anchoring extension's checkpoints in a Transparency Service, by reference to the anchoring extension at a fixed commit. Two worked examples: a software release decision, and an agent action capsule citing a decision.

section.name: Relation to the Decision Provenance Standard
section.t: This document is an independent, downstream description. It is not part of the Decision Provenance Standard, does not change it, and is not endorsed by its Steward. The name is used only to identify the Standard and its extensions, which are the source: where this document and the repository differ, the repository governs, and any change a reader asks for in a format described here is made in the repository first, as a pull request. The extensions are proposals in the repository; they are not part of the Standard itself.

"Decision Provenance Standard" is a trademark of Etsion Brands Ltd., used here to identify the Standard, with attribution: The Decision Provenance Standard, Yohay Etsion, 2026, CC-BY 4.0, https://decisionprovenancestandard.org.

section.name: Versions and commit
section.t: This document is written against the extensions as they stand on the repository's main branch at commit 5b0534d: anchoring 0.2.0, signatures 0.2.0, portable verification 0.3.0 and action binding 0.3.0, each a proposal written against Core v1.3 rev. 11 and the reference files 5.2.0. The names of are those the extensions index declares at the same commit . Each extension states its version in every document it defines; this document names them so that a reader can check the same tree.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

Decision record, action-binding attachment, stage, checkpoint, witness, trust policy and verification report are used as the Standard and its extensions define them. Signed Statement, Transparency Service and Receipt are used as and define them. Build attestation, provenance predicate and bill of materials are used as , and define them.

section.name: What the decision layer adds
section.t: A verifier holding an action record (a release statement, a build attestation, a capsule) and the decision record and attachment it cites can establish, offline:

li.t: where the approver's signature is carried, that the approver signed the outcome stage with a key the verifier's own trust policy maps to a person in role person; the authority reference that points into the deployer's charter stays the issuer's statement unless the verifier checks it against an independent source, such as the permission system;

that the specification the attachment says was shown to the approver, the one approved, the one that was requested, re-checked and executed, are one and the same, by equal digests, or exactly where they differ; for a release, that specification names the artifact digest, the bill of materials digest, the migrations and the rollback;
the options considered and the rationale as the record states them, with the time the rationale was recorded relative to the decision;

and, through the anchoring extension, evidence about when those bytes existed, each source with what it does and does not show: an RFC 3161 token gives a time from an authority the verifier trusts; a SCITT Receipt states no time, only that the service registered the statement into its log; an OpenTimestamps proof shows only that the bytes existed before a block was mined.

section.t: It cannot establish that the decision was right, that the action was, or what the reviewer actually saw or read: the check shows what the attachment says was shown; the verification reports of the extensions say so in every result, and this document inherits those limits.

section.name: Where it attaches in the software supply chain
section.t: Nothing here replaces a build attestation, a provenance predicate or a bill of materials; they say what was built, and they say it well. The decision layer sits beside them and is linked to them in both directions by digests:

li.t: The action specification the approver sees, carried in full in the attachment, names the artifact by its digest, the bill of materials by its digest, and the build by its identifier. A verifier that holds the SLSA provenance or the SBOM recomputes those digests and reads whether the release that was approved is the artifact that was built.

A release statement registered in a Transparency Service, or the build attestation itself where its format allows additional references, cites the decision record and the attachment by the typed digest references of . The SCITT Receipt then covers the decision together with the artifact.

A Transparency Service that registers the anchoring extension's witness checkpoints () gives each checkpoint over one issuer's chain of release decisions a Receipt from the same service the artifacts use. A Receipt shows the statement's inclusion; the anchoring extension does not yet check that the log only grew, so this is not evidence of an append-only history of decisions.

section.t: The stages an action-binding attachment records map onto a release pipeline without change: the proposal is the release candidate as the assistant or the pipeline drafted it; the review is the release manager's reading of it; the outcome is the approval under the release charter, signed by the release manager where a signature is carried; the request is the deploy job; the re-check is the permission or policy gate just before deployment; the attempt and the result are the deployment and what the target reported. A change of the artifact digest between the approval and the attempt fails the binding, by construction.

section.name: Artifact types for typed digest references
section.t: The Canonical Payload Binding defines a typed digest reference, {type, purpose, digest_alg, digest}, and leaves artifact types to the consuming profile; the Agent Action Capsule profile (section 9.1) asks that a declared type name carry a URI or reverse-DNS prefix. This document uses two, both declared in the Standard's repository under its own namespace, org.decisionprovenancestandard . The repository declares each name, what it identifies and which digest it uses; this document does not restate the digest rules and only says how the references are carried. A name never changes meaning; a different digest rule would get a new name.

li.t: type: org.decisionprovenancestandard.decision_record
digest: as declares it for this name, by reference to portable verification ; the same value as the entry's seal_hash.
type: org.decisionprovenancestandard.action_binding_attachment

digest: as declares it for this name: the plain SHA-256 of the attachment's bytes, computed as the action binding report computes its attachment_digest; not the sealed digest of the signatures extension .

section.name: What a verified reference shows
section.t: A reference that verifies shows only that the cited bytes have the digest it carries. It does not show that they are a decision record or an attachment, which one they are, or anything they state: that is for the document's own check, which reports it.

section.name: Carrying the references
section.t: In a capsule, the references are carried in references[] as the capsule profile allows, in the style of ; in an AgentInteractionRecord, in external_refs; in a receipt that keeps its object closed, as a separately signed claim linked by digest; in a release statement, in the cpb-refs protected header or in the statement's own payload. Nothing in the citing profile's protected header or verification changes. The cited artifacts travel beside the citing record, in a portable verification export and a signatures attachment, or are obtained from the issuer.

section.name: Verification
section.t: A verifier that holds the citing record, the decision record, the attachment and its own trust policy:

li.t: resolves each typed digest reference as CPB describes, and stops at Failed for a digest that does not match;

runs the action binding reference check on the attachment with the record, which reports the stages' consistency, the issuer signature where there is one, the time, and the pairing of the report with its documents;
runs the signatures check on the approver's signature over the outcome stage, where one is carried beside;
where it holds the artifact, the build attestation or the bill of materials, recomputes the digests the approved specification names and reports each agreement on its own;
reads the result dimension by dimension; it MUST NOT merge them into one pass or fail, and it MUST NOT report more than those checks find.

section.t: The reference checks, their cases and their vectors are in the repository under extensions/*/tests; this document does not restate them.

section.name: Checkpoints in a Transparency Service
section.t: A witness's checkpoint over a chain of decision records is a signed statement whose payload is the checkpoint's signed bytes under the anchoring extension's shared rule, with its Receipt, as the anchoring extension defines under "A transparency service as a checkpoint source" at commit 5b0534d. This document adds no rule; it names what a Transparency Service operator and a verifier need:

li.t: the statement's protected header : alg -19, kid the witness key's reference, CWT claims iss the key's holder and sub the chain;
the leaf: the statement's bytes as registered; a Transparent Statement is carried with its receipts taken out;

what a Receipt shows: that the service signed the statement into its log at a tree size; not the log's consistency, which the extension reports as not checked in this version, nor a registration time;

the registration policy is the operator's . A verifier never relies on it: it accepts only statements from the witness keys and chains its own trust policy lists for that service. A service may mirror that list in its policy.

section.name: A software release decision
section.t: The appendix carries a decision record for shipping release 2.3.1 of a claims-intake service, and the action-binding attachment of its deploy pipeline: the release assistant's proposal, the release manager's review and approval under the release charter, the orchestrator's request, the permission re-check, the deployer's attempt and the observed result. The approved specification names the build, the artifact digest, the bill of materials digest, the migration and the rollback. The record states three options and why the first was chosen. The action binding reference check verifies the stage dimensions; the example carries no signature, so the issuer signature and the time are not checked.

section.name: An agent action capsule citing a decision
section.t: The same record and attachment, cited from an Agent Action Capsule by two typed digest references in references[]. The capsule reference library parses the capsule strictly and verifies it; a verifier of the Standard resolves both references to the documents it holds. Nothing in the capsule's protected header or verification changed.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Where the approver's signature is carried, the decision layer authenticates the approver's act and binds it to the executed specification; an authority reference stays the issuer's statement unless checked against an independent source; it does not establish the truth of the decision's inputs, nor that the artifact a specification names is safe: that stays with the build attestations and the reviews they record. A relying party that needs a signed approval requires one in its own configuration and does not accept an unsigned attachment: anyone holding a signed attachment can remove its signature and present it as unsigned, and only a seal beside it shows that. Keys and sources of trust come from the verifier's own trust policy, never from the artifacts. A Receipt states no time; an OpenTimestamps proof shows only that bytes existed before a block was mined; only an RFC 3161 token from an authority the verifier trusts gives a time bound. The anchoring extension's security considerations apply.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document registers no media type in this revision. A later revision may register, in the vendor tree, a media type for the checkpoint payload, with the Steward of the Decision Provenance Standard as change controller; the content type stays optional in the anchoring extension.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts

abstract.t: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts prove properties of a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) to a verifier. VDSs and associated Proof Types enable security properties, such as minimal disclosure, transparency, and non-equivocation. Transparency helps maintain trust over time and has been applied to certificates, end-to-end encrypted messaging systems, and supply chain security. This specification enables concise transparency-oriented systems by building on Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and COSE. The extensibility of the approach is demonstrated by providing CBOR encodings for Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: An Agent Action Capsule Profile for SCITT

abstract.t: This document defines a SCITT statement profile for recording what an AI agent did: the Agent Action Capsule. A Capsule is a digest- committed record of one agent action carrying its verdict-level disposition (executed, blocked, denied, errored, timed out), the deterministic constraints that were evaluated, the effect that was committed together with a confirmed-effect binding that distinguishes a dispatched attempt from an observed result, and an honest human-in- the-loop flag. Capsules are identified independently of signing and MAY be authenticated by one or more COSE_Sign1 Producer Envelopes. Its Capsule ID can separately be made transparent by registration in a SCITT Transparency Service [I-D.ietf-scitt-scrapi]. A Capsule is recorded on every verdict, including refusals: a blocked or denied Capsule is the auditor-grade evidence that a gate worked.

front.title: Canonicalization Declaration for SCITT Signed Statements

abstract.t: Independently written systems that anchor records to a SCITT Transparency Service repeatedly need the same construction: a canonical form of structured content, a content-addressed identifier derived from that form, binding to a SCITT Signed Statement and Receipt, and references that cite external artifacts by digest. This document, referred to as CPB, specifies that construction as declarations rather than as a payload format. A payload profile declares its canonicalization algorithm and exclusion set and thereby obtains a reproducible derived identifier. A CPB Signed Statement carries either the complete statement content as specified by RFC 9943 or a digest of content held elsewhere using the COSE Hash Envelope of RFC 9995. CPB also defines an abstract typed digest reference information model and one optional protected-header encoding, cpb-refs; a payload profile may instead define its own reference serialization. An IANA registry assigns the canonicalization algorithm identifiers that these declarations name. CPB does not define payload content formats, establish or require a universal artifact-type registry, or require either typed-reference carrier.

front.title: Binding Per-Action Authorization and Memory Provenance into Agent Action Capsules

abstract.t:
The Agent Action Capsule (AAC) profile (draft-mih-scitt-agent-action- capsule) records what an autonomous agent actually did -- executed, blocked, denied, errored, or timed out -- with a structural binding that prevents an attempt from being presented as a completion. AAC deliberately does not define the authority that permitted an action; it carries that authority as an opaque reference. Two companion profiles supply what that reference can point to: a per-action authorization profile (draft-rampalli-aiagent-authz-hmac) records that an action was permitted (the "may"), and a memory-provenance profile (draft-rampalli-aiagent-memory-provenance) records the source and trust state of the belief on which the agent acted (the "why- believed").
This document specifies how the latter two are bound into an AAC Capsule. It defines (a) what the AAC "disposition.authority" reference MAY resolve to, (b) a namespaced, payload-only extension carrying an authorization-token reference, a memory chain root, and a quarantine attestation, and (c) an OPTIONAL divergence-class value, drawn from the per-action profile, that explains a non-executing AAC verdict. The binding uses only mechanisms AAC already provides -- the opaque authority reference and the payload-extension namespacing convention -- and changes neither AAC's closed protected-header claim set nor its Class 1 verification. The result is a single verifiable record that answers "may," "did," and "why-believed" together.

front.title: AI Agent Execution Profile of SCITT

abstract.t: This document defines a SCITT (Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust) profile for creating independently verifiable, tamper- evident records of autonomous AI agent actions. The profile defines the AgentInteractionRecord (AIR) as the COSE_Sign1 signed statement payload for material agent actions; maps SCITT roles to the agent execution context, with the Agent Operator as Issuer and an independent Evidence Custodian as Transparency Service; specifies Registration Policy requirements including hash chain integrity, temporal ordering, and sequence completeness; defines a redaction receipt mechanism for privacy-preserving evidence custody; and provides compliance mappings to EU AI Act Articles 12 and 19, DORA, NIST AI RMF, MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines, PCI DSS, and MiFID II.

front.title: A SCITT Profile for AI-Agent Action Receipts

abstract.t: This document profiles the IETF SCITT (Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust) architecture for AI-agent action receipts: tamper-evident, signed, offline-verifiable records of what an autonomous agent was recorded as doing at the governed boundary, under which recorded principal class, with what recorded verdict, and -- where the issuer records one -- under which policy identity. Each receipt is a signed record over a canonical JSON payload, hash- chained so that each record commits to its predecessor, and presented either bare -- the payload with its own native signature -- or enveloped in a COSE_Sign1. This revision specifies how such a receipt is carried as a SCITT Signed Statement, with the protected claims a Transparency Service requires, so that a receipt can be registered. Registration obtains a Transparency Service's signed proof that the statement was registered in its log -- a property a self-signed chain cannot provide alone. It does not, by itself, give an offline holder non-equivocation: that requires consistency proofs and monitoring of the log, which this profile does not specify. The profile makes a deliberately narrow, checkable claim: this is an issuer-authenticated, signature-verifiable, tamper-evident record of the action, the recorded principal class, the recorded verdict, and any policy identity the receipt carries. It explicitly does not claim that the agent was correct, safe, or wise, that the recorded inputs were true or complete, that a named approver authorized this exact action before it ran, that a downstream controller succeeded, or that any physical effect occurred. This revision separates those last three as distinct claims with independent failure behaviour, states the boundary of a shared action digest, and keeps a deterministic offline policy-replay capability out of scope.

front.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP)

abstract.t: This document describes the format of a request sent to a Time Stamping Authority (TSA) and of the response that is returned. It also establishes several security-relevant requirements for TSA operation, with regards to processing requests to generate responses. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Handling Long Lines in Content of Internet-Drafts and RFCs

abstract.t: This document defines two strategies for handling long lines in width-bounded text content. One strategy, called the "single backslash" strategy, is based on the historical use of a single backslash ('\') character to indicate where line-folding has occurred, with the continuation occurring with the first character that is not a space character (' ') on the next line. The second strategy, called the "double backslash" strategy, extends the first strategy by adding a second backslash character to identify where the continuation begins and is thereby able to handle cases not supported by the first strategy. Both strategies use a self-describing header enabling automated reconstitution of the original content.

front.title: CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims in COSE Headers

abstract.t: This document describes how to include CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims in the header parameters of any CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) structure. This functionality helps to facilitate applications that wish to make use of CWT claims in encrypted COSE structures and/or COSE structures featuring detached signatures, while having some of those claims be available before decryption and/or without inspecting the detached payload. Another use case is using CWT claims with payloads that are not CWT Claims Sets, including payloads that are not CBOR at all.

section.name: Appendix: the worked examples
section.t: The files are kept with this document's source (https://github.com/laurent-star/dps-scitt-decision-layer, examples/release-decision/ and demo/); the digests below let a reader check them.

li.t: Decision record DR-2026-0412 (record schema of the reference files 5.2.0, state closed): "Ship claims-intake 2.3.1 to production on 2026-10-23", three options considered, the first chosen; affirmed by the release manager on 2026-10-23T14:20:00Z. seal_hash: 34ba302a668e9200017a1083a92e88773dab1ca620faeaac8cd8bb7747596ba5.

Action-binding attachment (0.3.0, unsigned in this example): seven stages, proposal by the release assistant, review and approval by the release manager under the release charter, without signature in this example, request, re-check, attempt, observed result; one specification, digest 19ade2a46319ac6622333cd6731ac400ed11daa7d6955b5daa5864da91c2b711, carried in full, naming build 2.3.1+git.5d1c9f0, the artifact digest, the SBOM digest, migration 0042 and the rollback. Attachment digest: 5086c7674db770c6d01592ba697722a2fb468c16d1d5ab9226a7b5217c4bc1a8.

The action binding reference check on the attachment with the record: specification digests, record statements, action binding, stage order, authorisation re-check, observed results and rationale provenance verified; execution state attempted, result succeeded; issuer signature and time not checked, as the attachment is unsigned.

A capsule (format 4, action_type decide, disposition accept by a human, effect confirmed) citing both by typed digest references in references[] with citation_purpose ran_under and acted_on: capsule_id 8ffac39fe42e5d1b9dcbff838ec5c3aad749a3e8a32e3157791297f5f325b6e7; the capsule library (0.12.0) parses it strictly and its Class 1 verification passes with two informational findings (an effect type and a domain outside the seeded values); a verifier of the Standard resolves both references to the documents it holds.
